sentences.gloss_en: Hi everyone; to move our code from simple lines we read to strong systems built with a real engineering mindset,
the first thing we need is to picture what memory looks like inside.
Let's start the explanation right away.
OK, say we have simple code that says a equals 1, 2.
Then we said b equals a.
And after that we did a.append 3.
The question before we reveal the answer: what has b's value become now?
This needs a second of thought.
In short, the answer shows when we draw the stack and heap board.
We find arrows from both a and b pointing at the same object, the same node lighting up in the heap.
That's why b also became 1, 2, 3.
And here the essential difference shows up.
The equals-equals sign asks whether the two values are equal.
But is asks whether they are exactly the same object in memory.
That brings us to copying.
With a shallow copy, the outer wrapper is new, but the inner list is still shared.
So if we add an order to the copy, the original will also have 3 orders instead of 2.
But with a deep copy everything is separated; every level is copied and becomes independent.
So the original stays at 2, as it is.
This literally saves you from disasters of accidentally modified data in production.
And here comes one of the most famous and dangerous classic mistakes: the mutable default.
If the code defines the default value as an empty list like this: def f x, acc equals square brackets.
The scary problem is that this default is created only once, when the function is defined.
So it keeps accumulating data and fails in total silence with every call.
It grows from 1 to 1, 2 and then 1, 2, 3.
The right fix? Give it None as the default value, and inside the function create the new list.
Now if we do a quick memory-use comparison, we see the list tries to read all the data at once.
And the memory column keeps rising until the program gets killed, or an OOM crash, out of memory, happens.
On the other side, the generator yields one item at a time, so the memory column stays flat and stable.
To picture this huge difference in numbers: a million items in a list take about 8 MB of memory.
But the same million items with a generator take only about 100 bytes.
Can you imagine? That's a scary difference.
We're not talking about minor optimizations here; it's a matter of the system staying up without crashing at all.
Another nice thing is that generators compose together like a data pipe, or pipeline.
We fetch the data with fetch_orders, extract the data, filter orders worth over 500, add customer data, and finally save to analytics.
Each item passes through this chain step by step on its own, very efficiently, without using all the memory in one step.
OK, let's move on to the kinds of errors we can run into.
There's the syntax error, which stops the program from even starting.
And the runtime error, which crashes the program while it runs.
But the most dangerous kind, by far, is the logic error.
Why? Because the program runs perfectly normally but outputs wrong data and calculations in total silence.
That's what makes it a real nightmare to detect.
When an error or exception happens, something called stack unwinding happens.
The code pops the frames from top to bottom until it finds an except that catches it.
The order of the blocks here is very important.
We start with try, and if an error happens we go to except.
else runs only if there are no errors.
And the most important part of all this is the finally block, because it guarantees cleanup code runs, like closing files or the database, whatever the outcome.
That way we prevent any resource leak.
In real, large applications we always build a tree of custom exceptions and map them to HTTP status codes.
For example, PaymentFailedError gets 402, InsufficientStockError gets 409, and anything unexpected gets 500.
This organization makes a strong API that is clear and easy to work with.
The decisive point here is how we catch these errors in the first place.
The biggest engineering sin you can commit is using a bare except like this without specifying anything,
because it simply swallows the error silently and completely hides the problem.
The right way is always to catch a specific exception.
Log the error with logging and use raise from e to keep the original traceback and the real cause of the problem.
Sometimes we need to add certain behavior to a function without changing its inner code.
This is where the decorator comes in.
It's a wrapper we wrap the function with.
Like @timer to measure time, or @retry to retry on failure, or @lru_cache to save cached memory.
And always, always use @functools.wraps to keep the original function's name and metadata, otherwise debugging becomes a real nightmare.
As for managing shared resources, context managers are the best solution.
Using with DatabaseConnection as conn guarantees that the __enter__ function prepares the connection at the start and the __exit__ function closes it at the end.
Whether the work succeeded and we did a commit, or an error happened and we did a rollback, safety and avoiding resource leaks are fully guaranteed.
Now on to tests: if we look at this fixed red frame of a test that failed when run, that's not a problem, it's a necessary step.
Any test we write, we must see it fail first.
As we always say in engineering: a test that never failed never proved anything.
Maybe its code doesn't assert anything at all.
And as soon as we fix the code, the green frame appears.
The test passed, and now we can refactor, restructure the code, feeling very safe.
The basic pattern for building these tests is Arrange to prepare data, Act to run the code, and Assert to check the result.
It lays the foundation for any code we can trust.
These tests are divided into layers.
A unit test tests one function on its own.
An integration test tests components when they're connected and working together.
And an acceptance test is what checks that the business requirements themselves were met.
It's the only one that can detect missing data or requirements that were missing from the start.
Now we have a long traceback in front of us that can look scary at first glance.
Let's think together for a second.
Which line exactly, in all this noise, is the real cause of the failure?
The simple secret is that a traceback is always read from the bottom up.
The last line at the bottom is the actual problem that happened, and the lines above it are the path that led there.
The right debugging method follows clear steps.
Read the message from the bottom, reproduce the problem, narrow the search by changing only one thing at a time, use the debugger.
And finally, of course, document the fix.
And when we talk about the annoying Git conflict, let's split the scene into three regions.
Base, which is the file's original state.
Ours, which is our own changes.
And Theirs, which is the other colleague's changes.
Git isn't broken here; it just refuses to guess what people meant,
when two people change the same line, and it leaves the merge decision to us to pick the right one.
And the pull request, or PR, isn't just merging code and that's it; it's a space for collaboration and decision-making.
In review we ask ourselves: does the code achieve what the ticket asks for?
Does it handle the edge cases correctly?
And will anyone else be able to understand it 6 months from now?
And if we get lost in Git or lose a commit, the git reflog command is always there as an excellent safety net to recover anything lost.
We've reached the last stage, the culmination of all this work.
The final assessment gate includes clear achievements: 3 Python programs that run efficiently,
pytest results green over 90%, full documentation of a debug task, and 10 clear, useful commits.
This is where the real shift happens, from just writing scripts to professional, enjoyable software engineering practice.
In the end, what we come out with isn't just lines of written code; it's a merged pull request backed by strong tests, carefully resolved conflicts and documented decision context.
All these practices? Are we ready to write code that lives and runs steadily in a real production environment?
